Published by MW Editions, this new photobook by the lens-based artist Susan kae Grant is a haunting collection of whimsical dreamscapes—(re)constructed from her childhood memories and dream explorations, carried out at home and in a lab.

Divided into seven chapters,Night Journey comprises some 90 black-and-white photographs taken—or, the way Grant puts it, made—over the past two and a half decades, starting in 2000.

Except for just a handful of triptychs, with side panels shot on location in Europe, all images in Night Journey were meticulously staged by Grant in her studio. Here, she acts as a shadow theater director orchestrating scenes that are devoid of color and evocative of fairy tales, nightmares, and—probably—Plato’s allegory of the cave.

In some cases, it takes Grant months to create her tableaux as she builds intricate sets, adding and removing layers of props, instructs models, and repositions lighting. The result of all this artistic effort is dreamlike shadow narratives that exist only in imagination, within the photograph.

Within the book, photographs interplay in more ways than just being paired across spreads; some form intriguing longer storylines—triptychs hidden inside foldouts or overlapping images printed on translucent paper.

“In the lush blacks and milky grays that saturate these pages, Grant materializes ghostly figures, animals, objects, and sometimes woods to get lost in. She invites us into a cumulative, immersive parallel existence of forms both absent and present.”

—Trudy Wilner Stack, writer and independent curator

Night Journey sprouted from Grant’s fascination with dreams and the unconscious. First, she wrote down, sketched or committed to tape her dreams—right after waking up in her bed. Next, she enlisted a sleep researcher, Dr. John Herman at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. In his lab, Grant was awakened from REM sleep to record her descriptions of the dream space.

These explorations led to a decades-long artistic endeavor that—using shadow as a metaphor—provides a pictorial access to the unconscious. The project has been displayed through the years at a series of solo exhibitions and will culminate in a retrospective show and this book.

“My interest in the shadow lies in the notion that nothing is certain except the opportunity to imagine and create conjecture. Today, as an artist, my quest is to channel enigmatic aspects of life.” —Susan kae Grant

Susan kae Grantis a lens-based artist, educator, and early creator and curator of photographic book arts. Her studio practice and distinct personal vision are recognized as significant contributions to the history of fabricated photography. Her work is held in major museums and private collections, including the J. Paul Getty Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. Professor of Art Emerita at Texas Woman’s University, she is represented by Conduit Gallery.

Origini Edizioni publishes Pâle by Gabrielle Duplantier.

This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory.

Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic.

The black notebook symbolizes imagination, thought, writing, a place for ideas: the working notebook is black par excellence, always and across all cultures.

Gabrielle Duplantier is a Franco-American-Azorean photographer born in 1978. She lives and works in Bayonne, France. Gabrielle Duplantier studied fine arts and history of art in the university of Bordeaux.

Back then, photography, which she had practiced since a young age, was a mere pastime.

Once she got her diploma, she decided to become independent and settled in Paris, where she worked as a photographer’s assistant or as a set photographer. Parallel to her many collaborations with the press, publishers or musicians, Gabrielle Duplantier pursued her personal work on the female portrait, one of her favourite topics. Another source of inspiration is Portugal, her home country, which she visits on a regular basis.

It is the latter that we have chosen to present to you.

Private Reality– A Diary of a Teenage Boy

In 1976 aged nineteen while studying at Exeter College of Art I got my self a summer job on Weymouth seafront photographing holiday makers. I saw this as a wonderful opportunity to earn a living but at the same time doing a personal project showing the life of the sea side photographer.

Its about youth culture and being a teenager in the 70’s. Existential angst was preoccupying my thoughts.

It all came together through the lens as I was turning from a teenager to a young adult.

As well as the holiday makers I was photographing local people from the town, my friends, family and into the evening with the disco bars fair grounds and caravan parks.

I was also experimenting with abstraction through the graphic nature of photography.

It was my right of passage and coming of age and I started to look at the world through the camera.

The Cars – Sea View series

I saw these people in there cars, It’s a very British thing to do to drive to the sea side and (most probably because of the bad weather too) not actually get out the car but sea view gaze from with in that window. Its a bit like a camera you’re in a box looking out detached from the world taking in your experience.

So that observation and the inherent interest in my world around me along with my sense of humour and it was 1976 the year Punk hit the tabloids and Johny Rotten swearing on TV, youth culture was spitting at every one and doing V up with there fingers `I was a bit of a punk more in attitude than dress but it was I thought a bit ‘Catcher in the Rye’ by J. D. Salinger(a quote from google) ‘adolescents for its themes of angst, alienation, and as a critique of superficiality in society’ My friends at the time loved t˙is book I had the balls just to confront the people in there boxes and photograph them in the name of free speech and being rebellious, seeing the irony and humour and how they were maybe trapped in there cars and there lives. By doing this I was catching there unguarded reactions to what I was doing like utter surprise or confusion on their faces. I think it was punky a bit passive aggressive but harmless. Although the women you see getting out her car with the glamorous sun glasses and partner smiling came towards me and started hitting me with her hand bag saying ‘You can’t just go around photographing people without asking them’ but off course you can in a public space. I think I was like Ringo in Hard Day Night Beatles movie. Maybe I was escaping my reality rather than confronting it or its both.

Iain McKell

Von Lintel Gallery presents “The Surfing Landscape”. This multimedia exhibit pairs large-scale tintypes, prints, and a new film by photographer Joni Sternbach. This is the gallery’s third solo exhibition with the artist.

Joni Sternbach is renowned for her use of the wet plate collodion process, an early photographic technique dating back to the 19th century, in which a metal plate is coated with a silver salt solution, exposed in a large-format camera, and developed in a portable darkroom on the spot to produce an instant positive photograph, like the 1850’s version of a Polaroid. Sternbach is a master of this complex process, and the incredible clarity and size of her tintypes demonstrate her skill.

Sternbach’s use of the tintype process works on many levels; it fosters the collaboration between her and her subjects and brings people together. The images possess a unique and timeless quality, which resonates with the rich history of surfing and its enduring appeal. Although not originally her goal, Sternbach quickly became fascinated with the surfers who she first saw as obstacles to her shots of the ocean. She has been following them and their practice all over the world since then.

“The Surfing Landscape” features an assortment of Sternbach’s rarely seen mammoth works (14×17 and 16×20 inches). There will also be a selection of her complex, multi-panel tintypes (10×20 and 14×33 inches). These large-scale tintype portraits of surfers capture the rugged and raw beauty of their athleticism, and the spirit of adventure that drives them. The images are powerful and evocative, and much like the historical process that Sternbach uses, her photographs evoke a timelessness that transports the viewer.

This exhibition also features Sternbach’s film entitled “Making Pictures”, a two-channel, experimental piece about her experience making wet plate collodion tintypes in the field. Shot with a Go-Pro camera strapped to her tripod leg, this nine minute film is presented as a meditation about process, people, time, and space. Inspired by the transcendental film movement, it takes its cues from Sternbach’s own slow style of photography.

Sternbach is a native New Yorker. She received a BFA in Photography from the School of Visual Arts and an MA from New York University/International Center of Photography. Her work is held in many public collections including the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the National Portrait Gallery in London, the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, and the Peabody Essex Museum, among others.

Alexandra Mavros : The art of photographing hat slips away

In the work of Alexandra Mavros, an image rarely emerges where you’d expect. It is not built around the decisive moment, but around what comes just before or just after it, in those fleeting fractions of a second when reality momentarily stops performing its own role. Perhaps this is where the singularity of her gaze lies: photographing not the event itself, but its release. A Paris-based photographer and filmmaker of Greek-Canadian heritage, Alexandra Mavros has developed a practice shaped as much by cinema as by photography. The “fourth wall,” a notion she readily embraces, is more than a cinematic reference it is a way of seeing. Her lens is instinctively drawn to what happens behind the scenes: involuntary gestures, distracted glances, those subtle moments when the staging begins to crack and humanity quietly reclaims the image. Far removed from a fashion photography driven by visual demonstration, her work embraces accident, spontaneity, and observation. Soft, natural, cinematic light accompanies rather than dramatizes. Each photograph feels suspended, like a story deliberately left unfinished, inviting the viewer to imagine what lies beyond the frame. This search for a beauty inseparable from truth an acknowledged legacy of Peter Lindbergh is enriched by a discreet irony that recalls both Martin Parr and Elliott Erwitt. Her humor is never demonstrative; it emerges through details, unexpected juxtapositions, and coincidences that only a patient eye can perceive. Reading this Questionnaire, one thing becomes immediately apparent: Alexandra Mavros is as fascinated by the photographs she never took as by those she did. A Chihuahua in a stroller on the Croisette. A sailor smoking his pipe in the port of Naples. An elderly man with a sunburnt belly spilling over a red Speedo on a Greek beach… These missed photographs perhaps reveal her deepest obsession: capturing those fleeting moments that vanish before they are fully seen. At a time when algorithms increasingly standardize the way we look, Alexandra Mavros reminds us that “photographs are meant to be printed, touched, and leafed through not liked.” A simple statement that perfectly encapsulates her practice: attentive, demanding, and deeply committed to everything that escapes the relentless speed of contemporary images. For her, photography neither seeks to impress nor to prove; it simply waits for reality, however briefly, to forget that it is being watched.

Web Site:www.macrospictures.com

Instagram: @mavrospictures

What was your first photographic trigger?Alexandra Mavros: I was fifteen, holding my first camera, with my sister as my subject and my father by my side as my guide. He was teaching me how to master light, and to explain depth of field, he slipped his hand between my lens and my sister’s face. I pressed the shutter before he had time to move it away—and that was the real trigger. Photography suddenly allowed me to capture what the naked eye lets slip away: a hand moving too fast, a little sister who wasn’t grown up yet, and a moment no one else would have noticed.

Who is the image-maker who inspires you most?Alexandra Mavros: I’m terrible with first names—and even worse with making decisions. There’s Peter Lindbergh, to whom I devoted my thesis, especially his ability to unite beauty and truth. Then there’s Martin Parr and Elliott Erwitt, who are probably my favorite comedians. And Sayombhu Mukdeeprom, one of the first cinematographers whose vision made me look up his name in the end credits. I’ll stop there.

Which image do you wish you had made?Alexandra Mavros: Not one image, but a series: Lunchtime by Charles H. Traub. Candid portraits taken during lunch breaks in the 1970s. Color—and nerve!

Which image has moved you the most?Alexandra Mavros: A photograph of my mother when she was my age.

Which image has made you angry?Alexandra Mavros: Any image devoid of humanity.

A key image in your personal pantheon?Alexandra Mavros:Lovers. A tender kiss in front of the red-carpet barrier at the Cannes Film Festival. I pressed the shutter without breaking my stride I just happened to be there at the right moment. That photograph made me want to see my work printed large. I’d love to find those lovers one day and give them a print.

A photographic memory from your childhood?Alexandra Mavros: I was ten, armed with the family camcorder and pockets full of stories. I directed my sister and our cousins from England in our dining room. I dressed them, briefed them on their characters, and kept them acting until we couldn’t stop laughing. It’s one of my happiest memories. Twenty years later, I still haven’t stopped creating with my friends whether in a single frame or twenty-four frames per second.

The image that obsesses you?Alexandra Mavros: The one I didn’t dare to take. A Chihuahua in a stroller during the Cannes Film Festival. A sailor in uniform smoking his pipe in the port of Naples. An over-tanned octogenarian with his belly spilling out of a bright red Speedo on a Greek beach.

Which image changed the world?Alexandra Mavros: The one that came from the other side of the world.

Which image changed your world?Alexandra Mavros: The very first one I took with my grandfather’s old camera, then had developed in a lab.

If money were no object, which artwork would you dream of owning?Alexandra Mavros: My walls are covered with movie posters and family photographs. Once I have a blank wall, I’ll come back to that question.

In your opinion, what quality is essential to becoming a good photographer?Alexandra Mavros: Knowing how to let go and how to take the shot.

What is the secret of the perfect image, if such a thing exists?Alexandra Mavros: To make it. The Latin root of the word perfect, perficere, means “to complete, to bring to fulfillment.” A photograph that has been made is already a perfect photograph. And if I were allowed a second secret: synchronicity.

Who would you most like to photograph?Alexandra Mavros: Whoever is wearing colorful clothes.

Who would you most like to be photographed by?Alexandra Mavros: My grandfather.

An indispensable photography book?Alexandra Mavros: A Taschen book I bought at Paris Photo last year: the making-of of the first James Bond film, Dr. No. Cinema, photography, behind the scenes everything I love gathered into one object.

What was the camera of your childhood?Alexandra Mavros: The one on my first phone: a Sony Ericsson. The one I borrowed from my father: a Nikon F4. The one I eventually made my own: a Nikon D3100.

Which camera do you use today?Alexandra Mavros: A Sony A7 IV for its versatility. A Leica Q for traveling light. And a Canon Ixus 185 for the memories that end up in shared family albums.

Your favorite drug?Alexandra Mavros: Mastika.

How do you disconnect?Alexandra Mavros: Dancing with my friends in Irish pubs on Friday nights.

What question unsettles you the most?Alexandra Mavros: “How are you?”

What is your relationship with the image?Alexandra Mavros: Reciprocal.

Your greatest quality?Alexandra Mavros: Passing things on according to my astrologer.

Your latest act of madness?Alexandra Mavros: Joining a table tennis club in Le Marais.

An image to illustrate a new banknote?Alexandra Mavros: One of William Wegman’s Weimaraners.

A job you would never have wanted to do?Alexandra Mavros: One that wouldn’t let me do three others at the same time.

Your greatest professional extravagance?Alexandra Mavros: Printing on baryta paper.

Can photography change our collective perception of an event or an era?Alexandra Mavros: Absolutely. Photography can justify wars just as easily as it can end careers. But just as history books often distort or simply omit certain narratives, it is not photography itself that holds the power so much as the choice of what is shown and what is left unseen.

How do you perceive the influence of social media on the way photographs are created and perceived today?Alexandra Mavros: Like everything else, it’s a double-edged sword. As artists, we have more visibility and inspiration at our fingertips than ever before, but if we’re not careful, those very fingers can get cut off. We compose for the 4:5 ratio instead of the story we want to tell. We let the algorithm dictate our creativity, and when it doesn’t validate us, anxiety creeps in until we no longer want to post or even photograph. To avoid losing ourselves, we have to remember that the pleasure lies in the act itself, not in the “like.” Photographs are meant to be printed, touched, and leafed through not merely liked.

One Instagram account everyone should follow?Alexandra Mavros: @sciuraglam.

What’s the last thing you did for the first time?Alexandra Mavros: Getting out of bed on the right foot.

What makes a successful photograph?Alexandra Mavros: A photograph that has been taken.

What interests you most in an image?Alexandra Mavros: Recognition. Seeing something that feels true.

What distinguishes photography from art photography?Alexandra Mavros: The difference lies less in the photograph than in the wall it’s hung on. A picture of the tin of sardines I had for breakfast becomes art the moment I place a museum label next to it.

Which city, country, or culture do you dream of discovering?Alexandra Mavros: Brazil. Or Nepal. Or Indonesia. I’m not difficult I will happily go wherever someone is willing to host me.

A place you never tire of?Alexandra Mavros: Greece in the summer.

Your greatest regret?Alexandra Mavros: NO REGRETS.

Color or black and white?Alexandra Mavros: Color to attract. Black and white to undress.

Daylight or artificial light?Alexandra Mavros: Natural light until I discovered the flash gun.

In your opinion, what is the world’s most photogenic city?Alexandra Mavros: Sant’Angelo, Ischia. Full of color and elegantly dressed retirees.

If God existed, would you ask Him to pose for you, or would you rather take a selfie with Him?Alexandra Mavros: Neither. He’d probably be overexposed.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table?Alexandra Mavros: My mother, for love. Shams of Tabriz, for truth. Kate McKinnon, for laughter. Marco Bezzecchi, for the motorcycle ride after dessert. Howard Hawks, to film it all. And my friends, to complete the picture.

Which image best represents the current state of the world?Alexandra Mavros: The censored one.

If you had to start all over again?Alexandra Mavros: Less doubt, more momentum.

Last word?Alexandra Mavros: Gratitude.

MIA Photo Fair BNP Paribas will return to Milan from the 18th to the 21st of March 2027 at Superstudio Più, with a preview for collectors and the press on March 17th. Organised by Fiere di Parma and directed by Francesca Malgara for the fourth consecutive year, the fair will present its sixteenth edition.

The 2027 edition adopts Belonging as its central theme, following previous editions dedicated to Change, Dialogues and Metamorphosis. The programme will examine how photography addresses questions of identity, community and place in the context of contemporary social and cultural change.

According to the organisers, the concept of belonging extends beyond geographical origin to encompass relationships, shared experiences and collective memory. Photography is presented as a medium capable of documenting these connections while exploring the links between personal histories, communities and territories.

“With Belonging, we have chosen a word that resonates with many of the profound transformations shaping contemporary society,” says artistic director Francesca Malgara. “Photography is perhaps the medium best equipped to explore how we connect with people, places, communities, ideas and memories.”

The 2027 edition also introduces an updated curatorial structure. The Main Section will continue to bring together Italian and international galleries specialising in photography and lens-based practices.

The Beyond Photography – Dialogue | Work in Progress section will be curated by Rischa Paterlini, who previously oversaw the international FOCUS section. The programme will explore artistic practices that expand beyond traditional photographic formats, incorporating installation, moving image, archives and digital technologies. Participating galleries will present projects by artists from different generations whose work examines themes including identity, memory, landscape and belonging.

The Reportage Beyond Reportage section, curated by Emanuela Mazzonis di Pralafera, will continue to focus on contemporary documentary photography. Bringing together photographers from different generations and geographical contexts, it will present projects that move beyond conventional reportage towards more interpretative forms of visual storytelling.

Further announcements concerning the third curated section, participating galleries, invited guests, awards and the cultural programme will be made in the coming months.

**Applications for galleries are now open and will remain available until the 10th of December 2026, with an early application rate offered until October 20th.
